name: Lataguri
tagline: The highway village at Gorumara's gate
meta_description: Lataguri guide: base for Gorumara safaris, homestays and resorts, boroli fish, Jalpesh temple, Kalipur and tea gardens, with costs and how to reach.
summary: Lataguri is the village on the Malbazar–Maynaguri road where Gorumara's safari tickets are sold and most visitors sleep. It is a practical base: dozens of homestays and resorts, a few dhabas, the forest counters and the park a few minutes away.

local_story.title: Raikat country, then a road through the forest
paras: Before the British, the plains around Lataguri belonged to the world of the Koch and Rajbanshi kingdoms. The Raikats of Baikunthapur, a branch of the Koch royal family based near present-day Jalpaiguri, held much of this country from the 16th century, while Bhutan controlled the duars, the passes into the hills to the north. Jalpaiguri itself takes its name, by the usual account, from the jalpai, the wild olive trees that once grew here.

After the Duar War of 1864–65, the British took the Western Duars from Bhutan, and in 1869 joined them with the old Jalpaiguri area to form Jalpaiguri district. Forest was reserved, tea gardens were cut from the jungle from 1874, and railway lines and roads crossed the plain. Lataguri sat on the edge of what became Gorumara's reserved forest.

Its modern life began with the road. As Gorumara's reputation grew from the 1990s, the highway village turned into a strip of lodges and homestays, many run by Rajbanshi and Bengali families who had farmed and fished here for generations. Ask your host about his grandfather's fields; many will tell you about elephants raiding paddy long before tourists came.

did_you_know: Jalpaiguri district was formed in 1869, combining the Western Duars taken from Bhutan after the Duar War with the old Jalpaiguri subdivision.
The first tea garden of the Dooars, Gazaldoba, was opened in 1874; within two years 13 gardens covered about 818 acres of former forest and grassland.
Boroli, a small silvery river fish of the Teesta and Torsa, is so prized in north Bengal that it is sold by the piece in some markets in season.
intro: Lataguri will not win prizes for looks. The highway runs straight through it, lined with resort gates, a petrol pump, tea stalls and the forest office. But step 200 m off the road and you are in paddy, betel-nut groves and the edge of sal forest, with the calls of peafowl at dawn. It is where Gorumara's watchtower slots start, and that makes it the right place to sleep.

Most homestays here include dinner and breakfast and cost much less than the resorts. Families who run them usually know the safari drivers, the counter staff and which tower had rhinos yesterday. Use Lataguri as your two-night base for Gorumara, Chapramari, the Murti river and a half-day out to the Jalpesh temple or the tea gardens.
costs: Gorumara watchtower slot, jeep for up to 6
Car for a half-day to Jalpesh

highlights.title: Gorumara's front door
highlights.text: The forest department counter for Gorumara's watchtower slots is in Lataguri, so you can queue for unsold seats early, meet your jeep at the gate and be back for breakfast.

highlights.title: Kalipur eco village
highlights.text: A small forest corporation camp in the Gorumara forest, reached from the Lataguri side. Nights here are far quieter than on the highway, and a watchtower is close by.

highlights.title: Boroli and local fish thalis
highlights.text: Dhabas and homestays cook river fish in mustard and green chilli, with rice, dal and fried greens. Ask for boroli in winter, and for Rajbanshi dishes if your hosts cook them.

highlights.title: Jalpesh temple
highlights.text: One of north Bengal's oldest Shiva temples is about 25–30 km away near Maynaguri, with its linga set below floor level and a large fair at Shivaratri.

highlights.title: Tea garden mornings
highlights.text: Gardens lie between Malbazar, Chalsa and Lataguri. Walk the estate roads at 7 am, when pluckers head out with baskets, and ask before you enter the lines or factories.

how_to_reach.text: From NJP or Bagdogra about 75–90 km, two to two and a half hours via Sevoke and Malbazar or via Jalpaiguri and Maynaguri, ₹3,000–3,800.
Buses from Siliguri towards Malbazar, Maynaguri and Alipurduar stop at Lataguri on request, ₹100–150, about three hours. From Jalpaiguri town it is about an hour.
New Mal Junction (Malbazar) on the Dooars line is about 15 km away; Jalpaiguri Road station is about 35 km. Take an auto or car on to Lataguri for ₹400–800.

where_to_stay: Lataguri has the widest choice of beds in the Dooars, from family homestays charging about ₹1,200–2,000 per person with meals to private resorts at ₹2,500–6,000 a room. The forest corporation's Lataguri Eco-Tourism Centre is a government option near the counters, and its small camps at Kalipur and Ramsai sit deeper in the forest edge. Look for places set back from the highway, and avoid booking only by photographs: ask about hot water, generator backup and how far the room is from the road.
tips: Book Gorumara slots online before you arrive; the Lataguri counter only sells what is left.
Do not walk on the highway through the forest after dark; elephants and gaur cross it.
Ask your homestay to fix the safari jeep the evening before, with a pickup time.
Weekends and the Puja holidays fill Lataguri with Bengal families; weekdays are calmer and cheaper.
Carry cash for jeeps and tips; the village ATM is not reliable on weekends.

experiences.title: Half-day to the Jalpesh Shiva temple
experiences.summary: Jalpesh, near Maynaguri, is one of the oldest and most visited Shiva temples of north Bengal, with its linga in a pit below floor level. It is about 25–30 km from Lataguri and makes a good half-day between safari slots.
body: The temple stands among fields a few kilometres from Maynaguri town. Local histories credit its building to the Koch kings of Cooch Behar in the 17th century and later rebuilding to the Raikats of Baikunthapur, and it has been repaired several times since; treat precise dates you hear with care. Its dome and white walls rise above a large tank and the open grounds where the Shivaratri fair is held.

Inside, the linga lies below the floor in a pit, and devotees step down to pour water and offer flowers. On ordinary mornings the temple is calm, with local families, priests and a few stalls selling offerings. At Maha Shivaratri in February or March and through the month of Shravan, it is packed with pilgrims, many of whom carry Teesta water on foot.

Leave shoes at a stall near the gate, dress modestly and follow the queue. Photography inside the sanctum is usually not allowed. On the way back, stop in Maynaguri market for sweets or a quick lunch before an afternoon watchtower slot.

faqs.q: How far is Jalpesh from Lataguri?
faqs.a: About 25–30 km, 45 minutes to an hour by car via Maynaguri. A car for the half-day costs roughly ₹1,500–2,000. Local buses and shared autos run from Maynaguri, but a car lets you fit the visit between a morning and an afternoon safari.

faqs.q: What is special about Jalpesh temple?
faqs.a: It is among north Bengal's oldest and most important Shiva shrines, with the linga set in a pit below floor level, and it draws one of the region's biggest fairs at Maha Shivaratri. Its history ties it to the Koch kings of Cooch Behar and the Raikats of Baikunthapur.

faqs.q: When is Jalpesh temple open?
faqs.a: The temple is open daily from early morning to evening, with a break around midday on some days. Timings shift around festivals. Mornings are calm and best for a visit. At Shivaratri expect long queues and road jams for kilometres around.

experiences.title: Boroli fish and a Dooars thali
experiences.summary: Lataguri's homestays and dhabas cook the river fish of north Bengal, above all boroli, a small silvery fish from the Teesta and Torsa. A plate with rice, dal, fried greens and mustard fish curry is the cheapest good meal in the Dooars.
body: Boroli is a small, bony river fish that north Bengal treats as a delicacy, cooked whole in a thin mustard and green chilli gravy or fried crisp. It is seasonal and depends on the rivers, so it appears most in the cooler months and can be scarce after floods. When it is on the menu, order it; locals will tell you it has to be eaten the day it is caught.

A Dooars thali at a dhaba or homestay typically means rice, dal, a fried vegetable or two, a green leaf dish, a fish or chicken curry and a sour chutney. Rajbanshi households, the old farming community of these plains, also cook dishes with local greens, dried fish and sidol, a fermented fish preparation; ask your host if they make any at home, and try it with an open mind.

Vegetarians eat well too: ask for shak (greens), dal, potato and seasonal vegetables. Most homestays include dinner, so tell them early if you want fish rather than chicken, so they can buy from the morning market.

faqs.q: What is boroli fish?
faqs.a: Boroli is a small silvery river fish of north Bengal's Teesta, Torsa and their tributaries, prized for its delicate taste. It is usually cooked whole in mustard gravy or fried. It is seasonal and not always available, especially after floods; ask your homestay or the dhaba a day ahead.

faqs.q: Is there vegetarian food in Lataguri?
faqs.a: Yes. Every homestay and dhaba can make a vegetarian thali with rice, roti, dal, seasonal vegetables, greens and pickles. Tell your host when you book. Pure-vegetarian restaurants are few, so if you avoid kitchen sharing with meat and fish, ask how food is prepared.

faqs.q: What is sidol?
faqs.a: Sidol, also spelt shidal, is a fermented fish preparation traditional in Rajbanshi and other communities of north Bengal and Assam, usually made into a sharp chutney with chilli. Its smell is strong and its taste powerful. Ask your host; some families make it at home.

experiences.title: A morning walk through Dooars tea gardens
experiences.summary: Between Malbazar, Chalsa and Lataguri, flat tea gardens with tall shade trees stretch to the foot of the hills. Walk the estate roads early, when pluckers go out to the sections, and learn how Dooars tea differs from Darjeeling's.
body: The Dooars grow tea on the plains and the first foothills, mostly at 100–300 m, in contrast to Darjeeling's steep slopes. The bushes are lower, the shade trees taller, and most production is CTC tea, the strong granular kind that goes into Indian milk tea. The first Dooars garden opened at Gazaldoba in 1874, and by the early 20th century the district had become one of India's major tea regions.

A morning walk on the estate roads shows the rhythm of a garden: pluckers heading to the sections with baskets, supervisors with registers, the factory steaming in the distance. Many workers' families descend from people recruited from Chota Nagpur in the late 19th century; ask your guide about the garden's history and its festivals, such as Karam in August or September.

Gardens are private property and workplaces. Walk on public estate roads or with a guide or garden staff, ask before photographing anyone, and do not enter factories without permission. Factory visits depend on the day's work; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can we visit a tea factory near Lataguri?
faqs.a: Some gardens allow visitors on request during the manufacturing season, roughly March to November, but there is no regular public tour. Ask your homestay, who may know the garden staff. Factories may say no on busy days. Never walk into a factory without permission.

faqs.q: How is Dooars tea different from Darjeeling tea?
faqs.a: Dooars tea grows on the plains and low foothills and is mostly CTC, a strong, quick-brewing tea used for milk chai. Darjeeling tea grows at higher altitudes, is mostly orthodox leaf tea and has a protected name. Both regions were opened by the British in the 19th century.

faqs.q: Is it safe to walk in tea gardens near Gorumara?
faqs.a: In daylight, on estate roads, generally yes. But elephants, gaur and leopards use tea gardens near the forest, especially at dawn and dusk and in drains between sections. Walk with someone local, stay on open roads and avoid the garden after dark.

experiences.title: A night at Kalipur in the Gorumara forest
experiences.summary: Kalipur is a tiny forest corporation camp in the Gorumara forest, run with the forest village nearby. With only a few cottages and no highway, it gives you a real forest night, with a watchtower close by and the sounds of the jungle at dark.
body: The West Bengal Forest Development Corporation runs a handful of small community-linked camps around Gorumara, and Kalipur is one of the most remote. It has only a few cottages, so it is quiet by design. Villagers from the forest settlement help run the camp, and meals, an attendant and, on some evenings, a local dance programme are charged separately on the corporation's tariff.

After dark you hear the forest: barking deer alarm calls, owls, perhaps elephants moving in the distance. Mornings start with birds around the clearing. Staff will be strict about not walking out of the compound at night, and they are right: wild elephants and gaur pass close.

Book on the corporation's website well in advance. Access is by car from the Lataguri side, and the last stretch is forest road. Check current status before you travel, since camps close in the monsoon and for repairs after floods.

faqs.q: How do I book Kalipur eco village?
faqs.a: Through the West Bengal Forest Development Corporation's website, which lists Kalipur alongside its other camps around Gorumara. Recent tariffs were about ₹2,000 a cottage with meals at around ₹500 per person a day. There are only a few cottages, so book early for winter weekends.

faqs.q: Is Kalipur better than staying in Lataguri?
faqs.a: For quiet and atmosphere, yes; you are in the forest, away from highway trucks. For convenience, Lataguri wins, with more food choices, shops and easier safari logistics. Many visitors split two nights: one in Lataguri for the counters and one at Kalipur or Dhupjhora.

faqs.q: Is there electricity and mobile signal at Kalipur?
faqs.a: Expect basic power, sometimes with backup for limited hours, and weak or patchy mobile signal depending on the network. Charge devices when you can, carry a torch and a power bank, and tell family you may be out of contact overnight.

faqs.q: Is Lataguri the best base for Gorumara?
faqs.a: For most visitors, yes. The safari counter is here, the park is minutes away and there is a wide range of homestays and resorts. For quiet nights, consider Murti or the forest corporation camps at Dhupjhora, Kalipur and Ramsai, all within 20 km.

faqs.q: How far is Lataguri from NJP?
faqs.a: About 75–85 km, two to two and a half hours by car via Sevoke and Malbazar or via Jalpaiguri and Maynaguri. A reserved car costs ₹3,000–3,500. Buses take around three hours and cost ₹100–150.

faqs.q: How much is a homestay in Lataguri?
faqs.a: Family homestays usually charge about ₹1,200–2,000 per person a night with dinner and breakfast in 2025–26. Private resorts with pools and restaurants range from about ₹2,500 to ₹6,000 a room. Rates rise at Puja, Christmas and New Year.

faqs.q: Can we see wild animals in Lataguri village?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Peafowl, hornbills and other birds are common in gardens, and elephants and gaur occasionally cross the highway or enter fields near the forest. Never approach them. Real sightings of rhinos and gaur need a watchtower slot inside Gorumara.

faqs.q: Is Lataguri open in the monsoon?
faqs.a: The village and many homestays stay open, but Gorumara and the other parks close from about 16 June to 15 September. Some resorts offer low rates for rainy weekends and tea garden walks. Expect heavy rain, insects and possible road flooding.

faqs.q: Are there ATMs and shops in Lataguri?
faqs.a: There are small shops, tea stalls and at least one ATM, but it can run out on weekends and holidays. Malbazar, about 15 km away, has more banks and a larger market. Carry enough cash for safaris and tips from Siliguri.

faqs.q: Is the highway through Lataguri dangerous?
faqs.a: It is a busy road through forest, with trucks at night and speed limits for wildlife. Walking along it after dark is a bad idea, both because of traffic and because elephants cross. Use your lodge's car for any evening trips.

faqs.q: What can we do in Lataguri besides safaris?
faqs.a: Visit the Jalpesh temple, walk tea garden roads at dawn, eat boroli fish, spend an afternoon on the Murti riverbed and watch the forest department's elephants at Dhupjhora. Samsing and Suntalekhola are an hour away in the hills.

faqs.q: How many days do we need in Lataguri?
faqs.a: Two nights is right for most people: it fits two or three Gorumara watchtower slots, a Chapramari visit and a Murti evening. Add a third night for Samsing as a day trip, or move on to Jaldapara, about two hours east.
